title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K — fixed-size window, add right, subtract left.
shortTitle: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K — Fixed-Size Window, Add Right, Subtract Left

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of a fixed length K. The fixed-size sliding window computes the sum of the first K elements, then slides by adding the next element and subtracting the one that falls out of the window, tracking the maximum, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space instead of recomputing each window in O(K).
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the three-day stretch with the highest total deposits this week. Rajesh totals the first three days, then for each new day he adds that day and removes the day that slid out of the window, always remembering the biggest three-day total he has seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a running window sum by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one, and track the maximum — O(n), not O(n times K).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of a fixed length K. The fixed-size sliding window computes the sum of the first K elements, then slides by adding the next element and subtracting the one that falls out of the window, tracking the maximum, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space instead of recomputing each window in O(K).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants the three-day stretch with the highest total deposits this week. Rajesh totals the first three days, then for each new day he adds that day and removes the day that slid out of the window, always remembering the biggest three-day total he has seen.

**One line to remember:** Keep a running window sum by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one, and track the maximum — O(n), not O(n times K).

sections.s2_technical:
First compute the sum of the first K elements as the initial window and set it as the current maximum. Then for each right index from K to n-1, update `windowSum += a[right] - a[right - k]`, which adds the new element and removes the element K positions back in a single step. After each update compare against the running maximum.

A code snippet on daily deposits: `int maxSumK(int[] a, int k) { long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += a[i]; long best = sum; for (int r = k; r < a.length; r++) { sum += a[r] - a[r - k]; best = Math.max(best, sum); } return (int) best; }`. The subtraction of `a[r - k]` is what makes each slide O(1).

The improvement over brute force is the core teaching point. Recomputing each window's sum from scratch is O(n times K) because there are about n windows each costing K additions. The sliding window reuses the previous sum, changing only two terms per slide, giving O(n). This reuse of overlapping work is the essence of the window technique.

A senior nuance is handling edge cases: if K is larger than the array length there is no valid window, so you return a sentinel or throw. Use `long` for the accumulator when values can be large to avoid overflow, especially with money. Also, negative values are fine here because the window width is fixed; unlike the maximum-subarray-of-any-length problem, there is no benefit to dropping a prefix, so this stays a simple fixed window rather than a Kadane-style scan.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India marketing team wants to know Rajesh's best K-day deposit streak to time a loyalty offer, where K is a fixed promotional window. This is exactly how the maximum-sum-of-size-K window works — slide a fixed window and keep the best total.

Problem 2 — Deposit histories can be long, so recomputing every window would be too slow for a report that runs across many customers, which is why the O(n) slide matters.

The code shows a `DepositStreakAnalyzer` with `bestKDayTotal`, a demo on Rajesh's daily deposits, and the best window total.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: deposits [20, 5, 30, 10, 50, 40, 15], window size 3.

Step 1: The initial window covers the first three days 20, 5, 30 summing to 55. This becomes the best so far.

Step 2: The right edge moves to day with 10. We add 10 and subtract the day that left, which is 20, giving 55 plus 10 minus 20 equals 45. Best stays 55.

Step 3: Right moves to 50. Add 50 subtract 5 giving 45 plus 50 minus 5 equals 90. Best updates to 90, from the window [30,10,50].

Step 4: Right moves to 40. Add 40 subtract 30 giving 90 plus 40 minus 30 equals 100. Best updates to 100, from the window [10,50,40].

Step 5: Right moves to 15. Add 15 subtract 10 giving 100 plus 15 minus 10 equals 105. Best updates to 105, from the window [50,40,15]. The scan ends and the method returns 105.

```

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum sum subarray of size K asks for the largest total among all contiguous windows of a fixed length, and the fixed-size sliding window solves it in linear time. I first add up the first K elements to form the initial window and take that as my current best. Then I slide the window one position at a time, and for each slide I add the element entering on the right and subtract the element leaving on the left in a single operation, comparing the updated window sum against my running maximum.

The key efficiency point is the reuse of overlapping work. A brute-force solution recomputes each window's sum from scratch, which costs K additions for each of roughly n windows and gives order n times K. The sliding window instead changes only two terms per slide, the entering and leaving elements, so each step is constant time and the whole scan is linear. That reuse is the entire reason the technique exists.

I always mention a couple of practical guards. If K is larger than the array there is no valid window, so I return a sentinel or throw rather than reading out of bounds, and I accumulate in a wide type like long when values can be large so a money total does not overflow. Negative values cause no trouble here because the width is fixed and there is never a reason to drop a prefix, which keeps this a straightforward window rather than a Kadane-style scan.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a marketing report that found each customer's best fixed-length deposit streak to time a loyalty offer. With long deposit histories across many customers, recomputing every window would have been far too slow, so the linear slide kept the batch within its window. Explaining the add-and-subtract slide, the complexity improvement over brute force, and the overflow and bounds guards shows the interviewer I understand both the technique and its production details.
